why_this_format: The lesson is whether a route survives an interruption. Walking a labelled route, rebuilding it without labels, then recovering after a blocked door makes the player use place-order rather than merely choose that idea from four sentences.
trap_is_satisfied_by: Invented board geometry because the row supplies no compartment map. Eight declared locations have distinct landmarks. The normal route is control→radio→mess→berthing→auxiliary machinery→engine room→machinery control. Blocking the berthing-to-auxiliary door forces a detour that rejoins at auxiliary machinery, one compartment ahead of the blocked transition.
scene: The navigator sends you from control to machinery with a sealed note. On the return trip one watertight door will be shut and the marker lights will be off. You have walked the route once, with labels still visible.
assumes: a submarine is divided into named compartments
a route can be remembered as a sequence of places
task: Learn the compartment route, rebuild it without labels, then recover after one door is blocked.
question: Run the route from memory. After the blocked door, use the next landmark to work out where the detour has put you.
takeaway: A route remembered as places can be recovered after an interruption; a count or turn list usually cannot.
why: A count only works while nothing interrupts it. A turn list fails after one extra turn. A route made of places is different because each compartment becomes a new reference point. If you are diverted, identify the space you enter. Then rejoin the sequence from there. Submarines use the same logic when dead reckoning. The useful question is not how many steps have passed. It is what trusted reference remains after the interruption.
answerText: The recoverable route is Control, Radio, Crew Mess, Berthing, Auxiliary Machinery, Engine Room, Machinery Control. When the berthing door is blocked, the detour rejoins at Auxiliary Machinery, so you continue from there.

data.hint: Learn the labelled route first. On the second run the labels disappear. When the berthing door is blocked, identify the compartment where the detour ends and continue from that point in the sequence.

compartments.label: Ladder Bypass
compartments.landmark: vertical ladder with a brass rung plate

failure_feedback.action: following a turn count after the detour
failure_feedback.consequence: the extra ladder turn shifts every later instruction by one move
failure_feedback.line: Name the compartment you are in. Then rejoin the route from there.

choices: Own-ship machinery
A merchant on a steady course
Biologic sound
A closing contact
rebuttals: A source that follows our own throttle is ours. Nothing out in the water knows what our turn count is doing.
A narrow line at a fixed frequency, drifting slowly in bearing, is machinery on a ship holding a course.
Short chirps with no bearing rate, gone in a minute, do not behave the way a hull has to. That is life, not a contact.
Two lines an octave apart on a steady bearing, getting louder, is something closing. Steady bearing plus rising level is the one to say out loud.
scenarios: A steady hiss whose level rises and falls with our own turn count.
A narrow line at a fixed frequency, drifting slowly in bearing.
Short chirps with no bearing rate at all, gone within a minute.
Two lines an octave apart, bearing barely moving, growing louder.

why_this_format: Keep the matching screen, but remove the explanations from the answer labels. The old choices repeated the clue and made the match possible without interpreting the trace.
There is no authored instrument panel; the row already behaves as a five-option interpretation screen. Retyping removes a misleading format label without changing the intellectual work.
takeaway: Refraction can weaken a received path, but it does not selectively erase the source’s spectral content.
why: Broadband measures sound energy across a band. Narrowband looks for stable tonal lines. A sound-speed layer can bend a path and make an external source weak, but it does not selectively strip away machinery tones. Faintness and missing tonals are therefore separate clues. The layer can explain the weak level; the absent narrowband says no tonal line is above threshold. Eleven minutes of persistence argues against a transient artefact, and nothing aboard changed with the trace.

choices: A weak external contact with no resolved tonals
Own-ship noise
Biologic
A display artefact
Nothing to explain
choiceMechanisms: An external source can arrive weak after refraction while having no stable tonal line above threshold.
Something aboard would normally respond when our own machinery state changes.
A transient living source is less likely to hold one bearing for eleven minutes.
A processor artefact would not represent persistent acoustic energy on the broadband display.
Persistent energy on one bearing is not ordinary random noise.
rebuttals: Nothing aboard changed when the trace appeared, so own-ship noise does not fit the timing.
A brief biologic is possible, but eleven minutes on nearly one bearing is poor agreement with that explanation.
Broadband is receiving acoustic energy. The question is what produced it, not whether the display drew a line from nothing.
A persistent directional trace is evidence that needs an explanation.

why_this_format: The steady-bearing problem is a relative-motion interpretation, not an echo-ranging calculation. The old d = ½vt badge was unrelated to the reasoning and has been removed.
There is no instrument panel. The real work is interpreting whether agreement from a shared source counts as independent evidence, so a choice screen is the honest format.
scene: The chart overlay and electronic repeat agree to within one hundred yards. The depth sounder returns an echo after 0.120 seconds; sound speed is 1500 metres per second. The chart says 102 metres here. The last trusted position fix was 3.5 hours ago.
task: Decide what the agreement between the two navigation displays is actually worth.
question: What can you conclude from these readings before entering the banked water?
takeaway: Agreement only counts as confirmation when the second measurement can fail differently.
why: The sounder depth is half the round-trip distance: ½ × 1500 m/s × 0.120 s = 90 m. The chart says 102 m, so something is wrong by 12 m. The two navigation displays do not settle it because both repeat the same inertial source. Their agreement is one measurement shown twice. The sounder is independent, so the disagreement is real evidence. It does not by itself prove whether the chart or position is wrong; it proves the position needs an independent check.
assumes: an echo time is a round trip
two displays that share one source can share one error

choices: Treat the two displays as one source and obtain an independent position check before the bank.
Trust the two displays because they agree with each other.
Declare the depth sounder failed because it is the lone dissenting instrument.
Declare the old chart wrong and continue on the plotted line.
rebuttals: Two displays fed by one navigator are one measurement shown twice.
A lone dissent is not automatically a failed instrument when it is the only independent source.
The chart may be wrong, but the readings do not prove that. The safe conclusion is that the current position is not independently confirmed.

equations.about: echo ranging on a two-way travel time

answerText: The sounder gives 90 m, not 102 m. The two agreeing navigation displays share one source, so they are not independent confirmation. Get an independent position check before committing to the banked water.

scene: The sound-speed trace reads 1505 metres per second above 60 metres and 1485 below it. A contact held for forty minutes while this boat stayed at 20 metres, then vanished in one sweep while every other trace remained unchanged.
assumes: Snell’s-law angles are measured from the normal to the layer
a lower sound speed bends a ray toward the normal
why: At a layer, Snell’s law gives sinθ₁/v₁ = sinθ₂/v₂. For a ray at 60° from the vertical, sinθ₂ = (1485/1505)sin60°, so θ₂ is about 58.7°. The smaller angle means the ray bends more toward the vertical as it enters slower water. Across a real sound-speed profile, repeated bending can leave a region that rays from this depth do not reach. A contact entering that shadow can disappear abruptly instead of fading smoothly with range.

equations.about: Snell's law — why sound bends at a layer

answerText: The abrupt loss is consistent with the contact moving into a shadow region created by the sound-speed structure. Snell’s law shows the ray bending toward the slower layer.

why_this_format: The stop is about prerequisite order. Snell’s law is background context but is not used to solve the sequence, so the equation badge has been removed rather than pretending it is taught here.

takeaway: A structure has natural vibration frequencies, and forcing near one of them can make a small input produce a large response.
why: A structure has natural vibration modes. If a repeating force lands close to one mode, each cycle adds energy in step with the motion and the vibration grows. Blade rate is shaft revolutions per second multiplied by the number of blades. One shaft speed can therefore put that forcing near a hull or mount resonance while nearby speeds do not. That is why the practical fix can be an avoided speed band or a changed mount stiffness. The water-wave relation v = fλ is not the governing equation here.
why_this_format: Keep the interpretation screen, but remove v = fλ. This is structural resonance; using the water-wave equation here conflated two different wave speeds and mechanisms.

The crucial quantity is not the visible rise but the total inflow while a pump is already removing water. A ledger makes the player add the hidden removal term back in; a diagnosis list lets them guess the source without closing the rate balance.
replaces: the source-identification emphasis of m05.s1; m05.s2 is rewritten to teach the hydrostatic pressure driving the leak rather than repeating the same rate estimate
trap_is_satisfied_by: The visible accumulation is 88 gpm. Fresh-water loss and sonar-cooling loss are both 0. Those obvious countable streams total 88 gpm, not the true 143 gpm. Adding the hidden 55 gpm drain-pump discharge closes the ledger exactly: 88 + 55 + 0 + 0 = 143 gpm.
scene: Hallam has marked the forward bilge twice, one minute apart. It rose by the equivalent of 88 gallons a minute while the drain pump discharged 55. Fresh-water tank level and sonar-cooling flow stayed unchanged. Command wants the true inflow.
assumes: a measured level rise is accumulation, not total inflow
a running pump removes water during the same measurement
task: Read the flows, decide which terms belong in the ledger, and close the water balance.
question: How fast is water entering the compartment before the drain pump removes any of it?
takeaway: Accumulation equals inflow minus removal, so a removal already running has to be added back to recover the true inflow.
why: The bilge rise shows only what stayed in the boat during the minute. It does not include water the drain pump removed at the same time. The correct balance is inflow = accumulation + removal. Here that is 88 + 55 = 143 gallons per minute. The unchanged fresh-water tank and normal sonar-cooling flow contribute zero to the balance. A pump can make a serious leak look smaller on the deck plates, which is exactly why its discharge belongs back in the total.
answerText: About 143 gallons per minute is entering: 88 gpm is accumulating and another 55 gpm is already leaving through the drain pump.

data.hint: Read every stream for free. Count only quantities with the same units as the requested inflow. Remember that a removal running during the measurement does not appear in the level rise.

streams.label: Bilge accumulation
streams.display: 8 cm rise in one minute = 88 gpm

streams.label: Drain-pump discharge
streams.note: The pump was already running when both bilge readings were taken.

failure_feedback.consequence: the estimate omits every gallon the pump removed during that minute
failure_feedback.line: That is the rise, not the leak. Put the pump back into the balance.

title: What ninety metres puts behind the valve
task: Estimate the pressure driving the seawater leak
scene: The suspected hull connection is 90 metres below the surface. Ferro writes seawater density as 1025 kilograms per cubic metre and g as 9.81 metres per second squared. He wants the gauge pressure on the sea side of the fitting.
question: About how much gauge pressure is the sea applying at 90 metres?
takeaway: Hydrostatic gauge pressure rises in direct proportion to depth.
why: Hydrostatic pressure is p = ρgh. Use seawater density 1025 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s², and h = 90 m. The gauge pressure is about 905,000 pascals, or 0.91 megapascals. That is roughly nine atmospheres above surface pressure. Add the atmosphere already present, and the absolute pressure outside the hull is about ten atmospheres. This is why a small opening at depth can drive a large inflow and why the hull isolation matters more than adding another pump.
assumes: gauge pressure counts the pressure added by the water column above the surface value

estimate.prompt: The fitting is 90 m deep in seawater of density 1025 kg/m³. Use g = 9.81 m/s².
estimate.question: Estimate the gauge pressure at the fitting.
estimate.explanation: Depth multiplies the weight of the water column. The result is gauge pressure; atmospheric pressure is added only if absolute pressure is needed.

answerText: About 0.91 MPa gauge, roughly nine atmospheres above surface pressure.

takeaway: For an electrical fire, de-energizing removes continuing electrical heating and shock hazard; the burning fuel still has to be cooled and controlled.
why: An electrical fault can keep adding heat to burning insulation. The first electrical action is therefore to isolate the source and prove the conductor dead with a meter. That removes continuing electrical heating and the shock hazard. It does not guarantee that the fuel has stopped burning. The hot insulation must still be cooled below its re-ignition temperature. Ventilation is then controlled to limit oxygen supply and smoke movement according to the casualty plan. A hot bulkhead is evidence to monitor, not a fourth leg of the fire triangle.

why_this_format: There is no instrument panel. The row is a five-option explanation problem using readings already stated in prose, so CHOICE is the accurate screen type.
why: The scrubber can only treat air that reaches it. A shut damper can therefore leave one compartment outside the circulation loop while the plant outlet still looks normal. The handheld reading in berthing is supported by symptoms there, while handhelds elsewhere are normal, so the problem is local rather than boat-wide. The installed berthing sensor also disagrees with the handheld and the symptoms, which points to a second fault in that sensor. One failure does not have to explain every bad reading when the evidence supports two independent faults.

choices: Berthing is outside the ventilation loop and its installed sensor is also wrong
The whole boat’s atmosphere is degrading
The scrubber has stopped removing carbon dioxide
The handheld meter is reading high in error
Nothing to explain
choiceMechanisms: A shut damper isolates the space while a bad installed sensor hides the local rise.
A plant-wide failure would raise independent readings in several compartments.
A failed scrubber would show at its own outlet and across the boat.
A bad handheld would not explain local symptoms and the shut damper.
The local symptoms and conflicting instruments require an explanation.
rebuttals: Control and machinery are normal on independent handheld readings, so this is not boat-wide.
The scrubber outlet is clean, which argues that the plant itself is working.
The shut damper and local symptoms independently support a real problem in berthing.
A local symptom pattern plus a shut damper is not ordinary noise.

scene: Navarro has nine people in a 36-cubic-metre berthing space at 293 kelvin and about one atmosphere. With the damper shut, each person adds about 0.9 mole of carbon dioxide per hour. She wants the time for carbon dioxide to rise by one percentage point.
question: Using the ideal gas law, roughly how long does a one-percentage-point carbon-dioxide rise take?
takeaway: The ideal gas law turns a concentration limit into a number of moles, and a production rate turns that amount into a deadline.
why: A one-percentage-point rise means an added carbon-dioxide partial pressure of about 0.01 atmosphere, or 1013 pascals. Using PV = nRT, that is n = PV/RT ≈ 1013 × 36 /(8.314 × 293), about 15 moles. Nine people producing 0.9 mole per hour each add about 8.1 moles per hour. Fifteen divided by 8.1 is about 1.9 hours. The estimate is approximate, but it gives a planning deadline instead of the word “stuffy.”
assumes: gas pressure, volume, amount and absolute temperature are related by PV = nRT
the compartment temperature and total pressure stay roughly constant over the estimate

estimate.prompt: Berthing is 36 m³ at 293 K and about 1 atm. Nine people each add 0.9 mol of CO₂ per hour.
estimate.question: Estimate the time for CO₂ partial pressure to rise by 0.01 atm.
estimate.relationship: Use ΔP V = nRT to find the added moles, then divide by the crew production rate.
estimate.explanation: At nearly fixed total pressure and temperature, a one-percentage-point concentration rise is a 0.01-atmosphere rise in CO₂ partial pressure.

equations.about: the ideal gas law behind a life-support margin

answerText: About 1.9 hours for a one-percentage-point rise under the stated assumptions.

why_this_format: The stop is already about casualty organization. The instrument forces the player to keep one problem personally and give every other problem an owner, a first action and a return condition instead of merely matching canned assignments.
trap_is_satisfied_by: Invented boundary temperature and trend values because the row provides no numeric fire-boundary panel. Four problems are present. Only the aft fire boundary is both rising and capable of crossing an irreversible-damage threshold: 54 °C rising 6 °C/min toward an 80 °C insulation limit. Flooding is falling by 20 L/min net, atmosphere is stable, and the wrist injury is stable. Three qualified delegates and distinct first actions are available.
scene: The flooding is now falling because the pump removes 60 litres a minute against 40 coming in. A fire boundary aft is heating, the atmosphere is stable, and a crewman has a fractured wrist. The executive officer needs assignments now.
assumes: a problem’s trend matters as much as its present size
a complete delegation names an owner, a first action and a return condition
task: Keep the one condition that cannot wait. Delegate every other problem with an owner, first action and return condition.
question: Which problem do you keep, and what complete assignment does each remaining problem get?
takeaway: Delegation is complete only when an owner knows what to do first and when to report back.
why: The fire boundary is the one condition that gets worse fast enough to cross a damage threshold while you are deciding. At 54 °C and rising 6 °C per minute, an 80 °C insulation limit is only a few minutes away. The flooding is already losing twenty litres a minute net, so it can be watched. The atmosphere and wrist are stable. A useful handoff gives each problem an owner, a first action, and a number that brings it back to you. “Watch it” supplies none of those.
answerText: Keep the rising fire boundary. Delegate the falling bilge, stable atmosphere and wrist injury with explicit first actions and report thresholds.

data.hint: Take one problem yourself. For every other problem choose an owner, a first action, and the reading or event that must bring it back to you.

problems.label: Forward flooding
problems.consequence: Report if level starts rising again.

problems.label: Atmosphere
problems.consequence: Report at 0.9% CO₂ or if symptoms appear.

problems.label: Fractured wrist
problems.consequence: Treat and clear the damage-control route.

firstActions.label: Take an independent handheld CO₂ reading
Splint the wrist and clear the passage

failure_feedback.consequence: at 6 °C/min the boundary can reach the 80 °C insulation limit before a routine report returns
failure_feedback.line: Keep the one that can become permanent while everybody else is reporting.

why_this_format: There is no instrument panel. The evidence is already summarized in the scene and choices, so CHOICE is the accurate format.
scene: Broadband rises across every bearing at once. A new 212-hertz line also appears everywhere, and its frequency shifts slightly when the seawater-pump speed changes. The weather and sound-speed profile are steady. One pump was started twenty minutes ago.
takeaway: A signal that follows an own-ship control is evidence of an own-ship source.
why: An external contact occupies a direction; an own-ship source couples into the array from the hull and can contaminate many bearings at once. The decisive clue is not simply that the line is loud. Its frequency changes when the pump speed changes. Something outside the boat has no access to that control. Weather or a sound-speed change would not track pump revolutions either. The broad rise and control-linked tonal line therefore point to machinery aboard the boat, which is both masking contacts and increasing radiated signature.

why_this_format: The old sequence describes an experiment but does not make the player perform one. CONTROL makes them change one machine, hold the rest fixed, then restore the suspect and confirm that the line returns.
trap_is_satisfied_by: Invented line-level response values because the row supplies no acoustic panel. The baseline line level is 74 dB and measurement noise is ±2 dB. Securing the seawater pump drops the line to 61 dB, a 13 dB response. That exceeds 3×noise = 6 dB. Each of the other three controls changes the line by no more than 2 dB. Restoring the pump returns the line to 74 dB.
scene: Four machines are running when a new 212-hertz line appears across the array. Only the seawater pump was started in the last half hour. Haruki will let you change one machine at a time, but sonar must report before each next change.
assumes: changing several variables at once makes a causal result ambiguous
a suspected cause should reproduce the effect when restored
task: Change one machine at a time, listen to the line, then reverse the suspected change to confirm the cause.
question: Which machine causes the 212-hertz line?
takeaway: A correlation becomes a causal test when one variable changes, the response follows, and the response returns when the variable is restored.
why: The log tells you what changed near the time the line appeared, but timing alone is only a correlation. A causal test holds every other machine fixed, changes one control, and waits for sonar to report. The seawater pump changes the line by 13 dB while measurement noise is only 2 dB. The other machines move it by no more than the noise. Restoring the pump brings the line back. That reversal is what turns a plausible suspect into the measured cause.
answerText: The second seawater pump is the source: securing it removes 13 dB from the line, and restoring it brings the line back.

data.hint: Change only one machine before each sonar report. Once you find a large response, put that machine back and confirm that the line returns.

failure_feedback.action: securing two machines before sonar reports
failure_feedback.consequence: the line changes but the result cannot identify which machine caused it
failure_feedback.line: One control, one report, then put it back if you think you have it.

scene: After the 212-hertz own-ship line is removed, a separate contact on bearing 064° resolves at 149.7 hertz. Boats of that class produce the same machinery line at 150.0 hertz. The operator asks what the small frequency shift says about range rate.
task: Use the supplied values to estimate the contact’s line-of-sight speed.
question: Estimate the range rate implied by the 0.3-hertz downward shift.
takeaway: A one-way Doppler shift measures line-of-sight relative speed; the sign tells whether the range is opening or closing.
why: For speeds much smaller than sound speed, the fractional Doppler shift is approximately Δf/f = v/c. Here the observed line is 0.3 Hz below a 150.0 Hz rest line, so Δf/f = -0.3/150 = -0.002. Multiplying by 1500 m/s gives about -3 m/s, or roughly -5.8 knots. The negative sign means the range is opening. This calculation now belongs to an external contact; an own-ship machine would share the receiver’s motion and would not show a six-knot relative Doppler shift.

equations.about: one-way Doppler shift as a line-of-sight relative speed

estimate.prompt: An external contact’s line is at 149.7 Hz. The class reference is 150.0 Hz. Use c = 1500 m/s.
estimate.question: Estimate the line-of-sight range rate.
estimate.relationship: Δf/f ≈ v/c, with negative v for an opening range in this sign convention.
estimate.explanation: Use the fractional frequency shift, not the absolute frequency alone.

why_this_format: There is no instrument panel. The row already presents a fixed set of readings and asks which explanation fits them, so CHOICE is the truthful format.

title: What 1.6 cubic metres of seawater is worth
task: Turn floodwater volume into a force scale
scene: The forward bilge geometry gives about 1.6 cubic metres of seawater aboard. Ferro wants the force scale before command chooses how much ballast water to expel. Use seawater density 1025 kilograms per cubic metre and g = 9.81 metres per second squared.
question: What weight does 1.6 cubic metres of seawater add, and what equal buoyant-force scale would offset it?
takeaway: For seawater, ρVg gives both the weight of a known water volume and the buoyant force on an equal displaced volume.
why: A fully submerged boat does not have a simple “tonnes per metre of depth” rule. Extra floodwater adds weight; depth change also depends on speed, planes and dynamics. Use the measured water volume instead. For 1.6 m³ of seawater, ρVg = 1025 × 1.6 × 9.81 ≈ 16,100 N. That is the weight of about 1.64 tonnes of seawater. Recovering an equal force through ballast action gives command the right response scale. A four-metre depth change alone does not measure added mass.
assumes: floodwater volume can be estimated from the bilge geometry
one tonne of mass weighs about 9.81 kilonewtons

estimate.prompt: The bilge contains about 1.6 m³ of seawater. Use ρ = 1025 kg/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s².
estimate.question: Estimate the added weight and the equal buoyant-force scale.
estimate.relationship: F = ρVg. The same ρVg form gives the buoyant force on an equal displaced seawater volume.
estimate.explanation: Use measured volume, not depth change, because a submerged boat’s vertical motion also depends on planes, speed and acceleration.
estimate.solution: 1025 × 1.6 × 9.81 ≈ 1.61×10^4 N = 16.1 kN, equivalent to about 1.64 tonnes of seawater.

answerText: About 16 kN, the weight of roughly 1.64 tonnes of seawater.

why_this_format: The old screen already describes a heat-transfer chain. CHAIN makes the player assemble the handoffs, inspect what each link transfers, and identify the governing weak link instead of only ordering four sentences.
trap_is_satisfied_by: Invented flow readouts because the source row supplies the chain but no numeric panel. Six links form a path of length six. The hot bearing is the obvious distractor, but it is not the governing link. The governing link is seawater flow at the final heat rejection stage, which is fifth in the ordered path and therefore not first.
scene: The bearing is running warm at its usual load. Haruki puts the cooling diagram on the table before anyone touches a valve: bearing, lube oil, oil cooler, fresh-water loop, seawater cooler, and overboard discharge. One link is failing.
assumes: heat must be transferred through every required link before it can leave the boat
a hot component is not automatically the failed link
task: Build the heat path in order, then name the link that governs how fast heat can leave the boat.
question: Where does the heat travel, and which required transfer is limiting the chain?
takeaway: A transfer chain is limited by the weakest required handoff, not necessarily by the hottest or largest component.
why: The bearing creates heat, but that does not make the bearing the failed link. Heat must move into the lube oil, across the oil cooler, through the fresh-water loop, across the seawater cooler, and finally overboard. If any required handoff is weak, everything upstream gets hotter. The current readings show normal bearing load and normal oil-side flow, but reduced seawater flow. That makes the final rejection path the governing link. Writing the chain first prevents the hottest component from being mistaken for the cause.
answerText: Bearing → lube oil → oil cooler → fresh-water loop → seawater cooler → overboard. The governing weak link is the seawater-flow stage, not the hot bearing itself.

data.hint: Put the heat handoffs in physical order. Then inspect the link readings and choose the required transfer that limits the whole path.

links.label: Lube-oil flow
links.transfers: carries heat from bearing to oil cooler

links.label: Oil cooler
links.transfers: moves heat from oil to fresh water

links.label: Seawater through cooler
links.transfers: carries heat across hull cooling stage

links.label: Overboard discharge
links.transfers: carries rejected heat into the sea

failure_feedback.action: choosing the bearing because it is hottest
failure_feedback.consequence: the player names where heat accumulates rather than the transfer that is failing downstream
failure_feedback.line: Hot tells you where the queue is. Trace what was supposed to carry the heat away.

why_this_format: There is no instrument panel. The revised readings support a direct causal interpretation, so CHOICE is sufficient.
scene: The lube oil and fresh-water loop are both hot. Seawater enters the cooler at 9 °C and leaves at 23 °C; its normal outlet is about 12 °C at this load. The seawater flow indicator reads 45 percent, and one of two pumps is secured.
takeaway: For a similar heat load, lower coolant mass flow makes each kilogram of coolant warm more, so the outlet temperature rise gets larger.
why: Heat carried by a coolant depends on mass flow and temperature rise. If the heat load stays similar and flow falls, each kilogram carries more energy, so ΔT grows. Here seawater warms 14 °C instead of about 3 °C while flow is only 45 percent of normal. The hot fresh-water loop shows heat reaches the seawater cooler. The large seawater temperature rise shows too little water is carrying it away. A small outlet rise would instead suggest poor transfer across the exchanger.

choices: Not enough seawater flow through the cooler
The oil cooler is fouled
The bearing suddenly makes much more heat
The oil-temperature sensor is faulty
Nothing to explain
choiceMechanisms: Low coolant flow makes the same heat load produce a larger coolant temperature rise.
A fouled oil cooler would keep the fresh-water loop cooler, not hot.
Extra heat could warm everything, but it does not explain the 45% seawater-flow reading.
One bad sensor cannot explain hot fresh water and the seawater temperature rise.
A 14 °C seawater rise at 45% flow is not normal at this load.
rebuttals: The fresh-water loop is hot, so heat is crossing the oil cooler into it.
The 45% seawater-flow reading directly identifies a downstream transport limit.
Several independent temperatures change together, so one oil sensor is not enough.
The outlet rise and low flow are both outside the normal pattern.

answerText: The limiting problem is low seawater flow through the cooler.

why_this_format: The choice is explicitly about a four-hour estimate that could be wrong. STRESS makes the player move the transit duration to its pessimistic end and see which quiet-running lineup still meets both acoustic and endurance requirements.
trap_is_satisfied_by: Invented lineup noise-reduction and endurance values because the row gives no candidate table. At the nominal 4 h duration, both Maximum Quiet and Balanced Quiet meet the 7 dB acoustic target, and Maximum Quiet wins on noise reduction at 12 dB. At the pessimistic 6 h duration, Maximum Quiet fails its 5 h equipment clock and Conservative fails the 7 dB acoustic target. Balanced Quiet alone survives with 8 dB reduction and 8 h endurance.
scene: The engineer has three quiet-running lineups for a four-hour transit. Each lowers radiated noise, but each starts a different equipment clock. The transit could stretch to six hours if the passage slows. Command wants a lineup that still works when the estimate is wrong.
assumes: a robust plan is tested at the pessimistic end of a stated uncertainty
quieting measures can trade acoustic benefit against equipment endurance
task: Move the transit-duration assumption through its allowed range and choose the quiet lineup that remains feasible.
question: Which lineup still meets the acoustic requirement if the four-hour transit becomes six hours?
takeaway: A robust choice is the one that still meets the requirement when the uncertain assumption moves against it.
why: At four hours, the loudest acoustic benefit is tempting because its equipment clock has not expired yet. The relevant question is what happens if the passage takes longer. Maximum Quiet gives 12 dB but only five hours of thermal endurance. Conservative lasts much longer but misses the required 7 dB reduction. Balanced Quiet gives 8 dB and eight hours of endurance. At six hours it is the only plan that satisfies both constraints. Stress-testing changes the winner because the uncertainty is part of the decision, not decoration.
answerText: Balanced Quiet. It gives 8 dB of reduction and 8 hours of endurance, so it still meets both requirements at a six-hour transit.

data.hint: Move the transit duration from the nominal four hours to the pessimistic six. A candidate survives only if it meets the minimum noise reduction and its shortest equipment clock lasts longer than the transit.

failure_feedback.action: choosing Maximum Quiet at the nominal four-hour estimate
failure_feedback.consequence: a two-hour delay carries the transit past its five-hour equipment limit
failure_feedback.line: Run the clock to six hours. The best nominal number is not the robust lineup.

why_this_format: The original matching screen named sonar-equation terms but never computed the equation. A short estimate is already a strong format and turns the equation into an actual detection budget.
scene: After the quiet lineup, target source level is 145 dB and one-way transmission loss is 55 dB. Ambient noise is 85 dB, with 20 dB of array gain. The operator needs 10 dB signal-to-noise ratio for detection.
task: Compute the passive-sonar signal-to-noise ratio and the margin above threshold.
question: How many decibels of detection margin does the current lineup have?
takeaway: Passive detection is a one-way budget: source level minus one transmission loss and effective noise, with array gain helping the receiver.
why: Passive sonar listens to a source rather than an echo, so transmission loss appears once and there is no target-strength term. The budget is SNR = SL − TL − (NL − AG). Here that is 145 − 55 − (85 − 20) = 25 dB. The operator needs 10 dB, so the signal excess is 15 dB. This is different from the active echo equation, which has two transmission-loss legs and a target-strength term. The distinction matters because the old equation badge was an active-sonar formula on a passive-sonar lesson.
assumes: passive sonar receives a one-way signal from a source
array gain reduces the effective noise seen by a directional receiver

estimate.prompt: SL = 145 dB, TL = 55 dB, NL = 85 dB, AG = 20 dB, and DT = 10 dB.
estimate.question: Estimate the passive-sonar signal excess above threshold.
estimate.relationship: SNR = SL − TL − (NL − AG). Signal excess = SNR − DT.
estimate.explanation: Passive sonar has one propagation leg. Array gain lowers effective noise; target strength does not appear because there is no echo.

equations.about: passive sonar equation as a one-way detection budget

answerText: 25 dB SNR, which is 15 dB above the 10 dB detection threshold.

why_this_format: This stop is explicitly about the difference between a checklist claim and the physical condition. ATTEST makes verification scarce, so the player must spend checks on the signed claims whose failure would matter most.
trap_is_satisfied_by: Invented claim backing and present-condition outcomes because the row supplies no verification records. There are four claims and only two physical verifications. Two critical claims are unbacked: the hull valve and escape route. A third critical claim, drain-pump pressure, has a current backed test. Thus the verification budget is smaller than the list, includes critical unbacked claims, and also includes a critical claim that is already backed.
scene: The rig-for-dive sheet has four signed claims. A hull valve operates; every bilge has a baseline; the drain pump builds pressure; both escape routes are clear. You have time to physically verify only two before the dive.
assumes: a signature records a claim made earlier
a physical verification can fail even when the record is signed
task: Choose which two signed claims to verify physically before the boat dives.
question: Where should the two verification checks be spent?
takeaway: A signed record is evidence about what someone reported; it is not the same thing as the physical condition now.
why: A checklist compresses work into claims, but not all claims deserve the same verification effort. The drain pump has a recent pressure test, and the bilge baseline has a current logged reading. The hull valve has only a signature from last week, while the escape route can be blocked by stores after the sheet is signed. Those two conditions can hurt immediately if they are wrong and neither has current physical backing. With only two checks, verify the critical unbacked claims rather than rechecking the best-documented items.
answerText: Verify the hull valve through its travel and physically walk both escape routes. The pump pressure test and bilge baseline already have current backing.

data.hint: You can open each claim and see what evidence backs it. You have two checks. Spend them where a wrong present condition would matter most and the record does not already have current physical evidence.

claims.label: Hull valve operates through full travel
claims.truth: one valve is stiff near shut

claims.label: Every bilge has a starting baseline
Both escape routes are clear
claims.truth: one route is narrowed by stores

failure_feedback.action: spending a check on the already-backed pump test
failure_feedback.consequence: one critical unbacked condition remains unverified before submerging
failure_feedback.line: A signature is not scarce. Your two physical checks are.

why_this_format: The yard can complete only two of four good jobs. ALLOCATE makes the opportunity cost visible: every fitted job answers one mission question and leaves another unanswered, instead of asking for a single best option with no resource trade.
trap_is_satisfied_by: Four one-slot jobs compete for two yard slots, so total cost 4 exceeds the pool 2. Four capability questions are present. Acoustic signature and independent depth evidence are required; atmosphere margin and flood-pump capacity are not. No required question is answered without selecting its corresponding refit.
scene: The yard can complete two major jobs. Pump isolators cut radiated power by 12 dB. An independent depth sounder adds a separate transducer and power path. Faster scrubber media adds air margin; a larger drain pump raises flood-removal rate. The patrol needs two capabilities most.
assumes: a finite yard slot spent on one refit cannot also be spent on another
the patrol has both a stealth requirement and an old-chart navigation risk
task: Spend two yard slots across four refits and make sure the plan answers the patrol’s required capability questions.
question: Which two refits make the patrol plan complete?
takeaway: A resource plan is a set of questions it can answer and questions it deliberately leaves unanswered.
why: All four refits improve something, so asking which one is “best” hides the real decision. The patrol must reduce its pump-dominated acoustic signature. It also needs a depth measurement that can fail independently of the existing navigation chain. Faster scrubber media improves a margin that is already long. A larger drain pump helps a casualty in which stopping the source remains the binding action. With two yard slots, the complete plan is therefore pump isolation plus an independent depth sounder. Choosing either optional improvement gives up one required capability.
answerText: Use the two yard slots on pump isolators and the independent depth sounder. Those are the two required mission capabilities; the scrubber and larger drain pump are useful but optional for this patrol.

data.hint: Each refit costs one yard slot. The panel shows which patrol questions your current pair can answer. You have only two slots, so a complete plan must deliberately leave some useful improvements undone.

answers.label: Can the boat cut its pump-dominated radiated signature for the constrained passage?
Can navigation obtain a depth measurement with an independent sensor and power path?
Can the boat extend an already-long carbon-dioxide margin?
Can the boat pump a severe flood faster after the source is attacked?

failure_feedback.action: spending a slot on an optional margin while leaving a required question unanswered
failure_feedback.consequence: the patrol enters either the stealth passage or old-chart navigation problem without the capability the plan assumed
failure_feedback.line: A good refit is still the wrong refit if it leaves a required mission question unanswered.

scene: The yard quotes a 12 dB reduction in the boat’s radiated acoustic power level from new pump mounts. The wardroom has described that as “about a tenth quieter” and is weighing it against the other refits.
takeaway: A decibel difference is a logarithmic power ratio: 12 dB corresponds to about a sixteen-fold change in power.
why: For a power ratio, ΔL = 10 log₁₀(P₂/P₁). A 12 dB reduction means the original-to-new power ratio is 10^(12/10) ≈ 15.85. So the new radiated power is about 1/15.85, or 6.3 percent, of the old value. The common “3 dB is a doubling” shortcut gives nearly the same answer: four 3 dB steps are about a factor of sixteen. The exact logarithmic calculation is better here because the equation is what the course is supposed to teach.
assumes: decibels here are being used for an acoustic power ratio

estimate.prompt: The mounts reduce radiated acoustic power level by 12 dB.
estimate.question: By what factor is radiated power reduced?
estimate.relationship: Reduction factor = 10^(ΔL/10) for a power-level difference in decibels.
estimate.explanation: A logarithmic level difference turns subtraction in decibels into a power ratio.
estimate.solution: 10^(12/10) = 10^1.2 ≈ 15.85, so the power is about sixteen times lower, or 6.3% of the original.
labels: 3 dB  (about a factor of two, for scale)

answerText: A factor of about 15.85, usually rounded to sixteen; the new radiated power is about 6.3% of the old value.

scene: The proposed second sounder costs £2.4m and has its own transducer and power path. The existing depth display and its repeater both use one transducer, so those two readings can agree even if that shared source is wrong.
question: What does the independent second sounder actually buy?
takeaway: Redundancy is valuable when the backup has a different failure path, not merely another display.
why: Two displays fed by one transducer are not two independent measurements. They can agree perfectly while sharing the same sensor error, power fault or calibration problem. A second sounder with its own transducer and power path adds a genuinely different failure mode. It does not make either instrument more precise. It also does not guarantee the chart is right. It gives command a second physical measurement that can disagree for a meaningful reason. That is how a bad shared source gets detected instead of repeated.
assumes: two displays sharing one sensor share that sensor’s failures

why_this_format: There is no instrument panel. This is a synthesis choice using five stated conditions, so CHOICE is the accurate screen type.
assumes: trend and time-to-limit matter more than whether a reading merely looks abnormal

why_this_format: The old multiple choice gives away the answer because the correct option literally names “the difference of their frequencies.” A short estimate makes the player calculate the beat rate and then connects it to wavelength and phase.
scene: Two narrowband components sit at 147 and 150 hertz on the same bearing. In seawater the sound speed is about 1500 metres per second. The audio level swells and fades regularly while both spectral lines themselves remain steady.
task: Calculate the beat frequency and connect it to the two wavelengths.
question: How many amplitude swells per second should the two tones produce?
takeaway: Two nearby frequencies beat at their difference frequency because their relative phase cycles steadily.
why: The beat frequency is fbeat = |f₁ − f₂|, so 150 − 147 = 3 Hz: three amplitude swells each second. The wave relation v = fλ also gives different wavelengths in the same water: about 1500/147 = 10.20 m and 1500/150 = 10.00 m. Because the two wave patterns advance with slightly different phase rates, they repeatedly line up and oppose each other. The pulsing is therefore interference between close-frequency components, not a third spectral line or a changing shaft speed.
assumes: waves add when they arrive together
sound speed is approximately the same for these two nearby frequencies

estimate.prompt: Two tones are 147 Hz and 150 Hz in water where v ≈ 1500 m/s.
estimate.question: Estimate the beat frequency. Then compare the two wavelengths.
estimate.explanation: The frequency difference sets how fast the relative phase repeats. The shared wave speed means the two frequencies also have slightly different wavelengths.

answerText: 3 beats per second. The corresponding wavelengths are about 10.20 m and 10.00 m.
